lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Do you want to knock on the door?

choices.text: Knock and introduce yourself
choices.npcResponseText: You knock once and give the resident time to answer.
choices.educationalNote: A respectful canvasser identifies themself, explains why they are visiting, and accepts a resident's choice not to talk.

choices.text: Not now
choices.npcResponseText: You can visit another home whenever you are ready.

lines.speaker: Resident
lines.text: Hello. What would you like to talk about?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Nobody answered. You can leave a respectful note or continue to the next home.

lines.speaker: Parent
lines.text: I really hope they expand the sidewalks. My kids walk to school every day.

lines.speaker: Neighbor
lines.text: I agree. There are too many cars during pickup.

lines.speaker: Business Owner
lines.text: The construction slowed down customers.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.text: True, but the new road should help long term.

lines.speaker: Student
lines.text: I didn't know the City Council actually voted on parks.

lines.speaker: Friend
lines.text: I thought schools handled that.

lines.speaker: Older Resident
lines.text: I've lived here twenty years.

lines.speaker: Older Resident
lines.text: You can really tell when the city invests in maintenance.

lines.speaker: Older Resident
lines.text: You canvassers keep coming around even when there's no election. That still surprises me, twenty years in.

choices.text: Explain that's the whole point — trust shouldn't only show up at election time
choices.npcResponseText: "Well. I appreciate that, actually." She smiles.
choices.educationalNote: That's the thesis of off-season canvassing: showing up consistently, not just when votes are on the line, is what actually builds trust.

choices.text: Admit it's mostly just before elections
choices.npcResponseText: "Ha. That's what I figured." She doesn't seem surprised, or impressed.
choices.educationalNote: This is the exact perception off-season canvassing is meant to fix — confirming it only reinforces the cynicism.

choices.text: Change the subject
choices.npcResponseText: "...Alright then."
choices.educationalNote: Avoiding the question is its own answer — residents notice when a conversation gets dodged.

lines.speaker: Cyclist
lines.text: I'd bike to work every day if we had more protected bike lanes.

lines.speaker: Transit Rider
lines.text: The bus is reliable.

lines.speaker: Transit Rider
lines.text: I just wish it came every fifteen minutes.

lines.speaker: Young Parent
lines.text: The library's after-school program has been amazing.

lines.speaker: Restaurant Owner
lines.text: We depend on community events.

lines.speaker: Restaurant Owner
lines.text: When there's a festival downtown, business doubles.

lines.speaker: Restaurant Owner
lines.text: Are you with the city? If so — this block could use more foot traffic outside festival weekends. Can you help with that?

choices.text: Offer to note it for the events office and follow up later
choices.npcResponseText: "That'd mean a lot. Most people just say 'I'll look into it' and vanish."
choices.educationalNote: Following up is what separates real canvassing from a one-time photo-op — off-season visits work because someone actually closes the loop.

choices.text: Shrug and say that's not really your department
choices.npcResponseText: "Right. Of course." He turns back to the register.
choices.educationalNote: Deflecting a fair concern reads as indifference. "I don't know, but I'll find out" builds more trust than waving someone off.

choices.text: Promise a festival every single weekend
choices.npcResponseText: "Every weekend? That's... a lot. I don't think that's realistic."
choices.educationalNote: Big, unrealistic promises can sound generous, but residents can usually tell — credibility matters more than enthusiasm.

lines.speaker: City Employee
lines.text: People usually only notice government when something goes wrong.

lines.speaker: City Employee
lines.text: But hundreds of small decisions keep the city running every day.

lines.speaker: Teenager
lines.text: I came here because our class has to attend tonight's council meeting.

lines.speaker: Friend
lines.text: I didn't realize anyone could actually speak during public comment.

lines.speaker: City Engineer
lines.text: Half of what we repair, people never even see — it's the pipe under the road, not the road itself.

lines.speaker: Passerby
lines.text: Huh. I always just figured potholes were random.

lines.speaker: City Engineer
lines.text: Since you're checking in — has anyone on your route mentioned anything about the repairs?

choices.text: Share what neighbors told you and ask what happens next
choices.npcResponseText: "That's genuinely useful — most of what we hear comes in only after something breaks."
choices.educationalNote: Canvassers are often the fastest link between what residents notice and what city departments can actually fix.

choices.text: Say you didn't really talk to anyone about it
choices.npcResponseText: "Ah, no worries. Just curious."
choices.educationalNote: Skipping the actual conversation defeats the purpose of an off-season canvass — it's the listening that builds the relationship, not just showing up.

choices.text: Complain that road work always takes too long
choices.npcResponseText: "...I mean, we're doing our best with what we've got."
choices.educationalNote: Canvassing works best as a two-way conversation, not a chance to vent — specific, constructive feedback lands better than frustration.

lines.speaker: New Resident
lines.text: We just moved here in the spring — still figuring out which meetings are worth going to.

lines.speaker: Park Volunteer
lines.text: We do this every season. It's amazing how much trash collects near the creek.

lines.speaker: City Planner
lines.text: Every rezoning goes through a public hearing first. It's slower, but it means residents actually get a say.

lines.speaker: Canvasser
lines.text: Hi! I'm not here about an election — just checking in on behalf of the city. Anything on your street that needs attention?

choices.text: Ask what's been going on lately, and really listen
choices.npcResponseText: "Actually, yeah — the streetlight on the corner's been out for weeks." She seems glad someone finally asked.
choices.educationalNote: Real canvassers lead with a specific, listening-first question. It surfaces concrete issues staff can actually act on — and it works whether or not an election is coming.

choices.text: Say you're just passing through and keep walking
choices.npcResponseText: "Oh — okay. No worries." She looks a little disappointed and goes back to her day.
choices.educationalNote: Off-season canvassing only builds trust if it feels genuine. Rushing past the one moment someone's willing to talk defeats the purpose of showing up at all.

choices.text: Promise the city will fix everything by next week
choices.npcResponseText: "...Next week? That seems optimistic." She looks skeptical rather than reassured.
choices.educationalNote: Overpromising feels generous in the moment, but it erodes trust faster than saying nothing — and it damages the next volunteer's credibility too.

lines.speaker: Canvasser
lines.text: We do this between elections too. It's easier to fix small problems — and easier to get people to city meetings — when we already know each other.

lines.speaker: Governor
lines.text: Thanks for coming in. I'll be honest — the check-ins from your team haven't landed well lately. People feel like we only show up when we need something.

lines.speaker: Governor
lines.text: Where should we focus next?

choices.text: Focus on residential streets — door-to-door check-ins
choices.npcResponseText: "Good — that's where word of mouth travels fastest."
choices.educationalNote: Prioritizing where to canvass isn't guesswork — it's usually driven by where trust has eroded most, or where an issue's gone unresolved.

choices.text: Focus on the commercial strip — check in with local businesses
choices.npcResponseText: "Business owners talk to a lot of people — good multiplier effect."
choices.educationalNote: Business owners are natural connectors — word travels through a commercial strip fast, for better or worse.

choices.text: Focus on transit riders and public infrastructure concerns
choices.npcResponseText: "That's often the most overlooked group. Good call."
choices.educationalNote: Transit riders and infrastructure users are frequently the last to be asked, even though they're directly affected by city decisions.

lines.speaker: Governor
lines.text: Good to see you. Things are steady — residents seem to appreciate the check-ins, even if it's not dramatic yet.

lines.speaker: Governor
lines.text: Where should we focus next?

choices.text: Focus on residential streets — door-to-door check-ins
choices.npcResponseText: "Good — that's where word of mouth travels fastest."
choices.educationalNote: Prioritizing where to canvass isn't guesswork — it's usually driven by where trust has eroded most, or where an issue's gone unresolved.

choices.text: Focus on the commercial strip — check in with local businesses
choices.npcResponseText: "Business owners talk to a lot of people — good multiplier effect."
choices.educationalNote: Business owners are natural connectors — word travels through a commercial strip fast, for better or worse.

choices.text: Focus on transit riders and public infrastructure concerns
choices.npcResponseText: "That's often the most overlooked group. Good call."
choices.educationalNote: Transit riders and infrastructure users are frequently the last to be asked, even though they're directly affected by city decisions.

lines.speaker: Governor
lines.text: Word's gotten around — people are actually looking forward to seeing canvassers this season. That doesn't happen by accident.

lines.speaker: Governor
lines.text: Where should we focus next?

choices.text: Focus on residential streets — door-to-door check-ins
choices.npcResponseText: "Good — that's where word of mouth travels fastest."
choices.educationalNote: Prioritizing where to canvass isn't guesswork — it's usually driven by where trust has eroded most, or where an issue's gone unresolved.

choices.text: Focus on the commercial strip — check in with local businesses
choices.npcResponseText: "Business owners talk to a lot of people — good multiplier effect."
choices.educationalNote: Business owners are natural connectors — word travels through a commercial strip fast, for better or worse.

choices.text: Focus on transit riders and public infrastructure concerns
choices.npcResponseText: "That's often the most overlooked group. Good call."
choices.educationalNote: Transit riders and infrastructure users are frequently the last to be asked, even though they're directly affected by city decisions.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.text: Three hours of walking and half the doors didn't even open. Some days I wonder if this is worth it.

choices.text: Ask what kept her going anyway
choices.npcResponseText: "Honestly? The two conversations that actually happened. One guy hadn't voted in years and asked how to start." She perks up remembering it.
choices.educationalNote: Volunteer burnout is real, and the antidote isn't pretending every door is a win — it's remembering the handful of real conversations that make the whole route worth it.

choices.text: Tell her the low response rate means canvassing doesn't work
choices.npcResponseText: "...Thanks, that's encouraging." She looks more discouraged, not less.
choices.educationalNote: A low doors-answered rate is normal, not a sign of failure — real campaigns plan around it rather than treating every unanswered door as a rejection.

choices.text: Change the subject to tomorrow's route instead
choices.npcResponseText: "Sure... I guess." She nods but doesn't seem heard.
choices.educationalNote: Debrief conversations are where volunteers process a hard shift — skipping past it to logistics can leave people feeling unsupported and more likely to burn out.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.text: Anyway — same time next week? I'd rather do this with someone else than alone.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: A guy yelled at me today for even bringing up city stuff. I didn't say anything about an election, I swear.

choices.text: Explain that off-season visits can look suspicious at first, and that's normal
choices.npcResponseText: "Oh — that actually makes me feel better. I thought I did something wrong." He relaxes a little.
choices.educationalNote: Some residents assume any doorstep visit is political, even outside election season. Volunteers who understand that reaction in advance take it less personally and stay in it longer.

choices.text: Suggest he stop canvassing that street
choices.npcResponseText: "So we just... skip people who react badly? That doesn't seem right either." He looks unconvinced.
choices.educationalNote: Avoiding a street after one bad reaction means the residents who most need a follow-up conversation never get one — a single hostile response isn't representative.

choices.text: Tell him to toughen up, it's part of the job
choices.npcResponseText: "...Right. Okay." He goes quiet for the rest of the conversation.
choices.educationalNote: Dismissing a new volunteer's discomfort is one of the fastest ways to lose them entirely — debrief support is part of what keeps canvassing programs staffed.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: I'll try again tomorrow. Just wanted to say it out loud before I did.

lines.speaker: City Greeter
lines.text: Welcome. The Council Chamber is through the Community Issues corridor on your left. The Mayor's Office is through the Community Resources corridor on your right.

lines.speaker: City Greeter
lines.text: You can review the community plan, explore the civic exhibits, and finish in the Reflection Hall. The neighborhood doors are there when you're ready to listen and canvass.

lines.speaker: Mayor Rivera
lines.text: Welcome. Our current community plan focuses on safe routes to school, accessible sidewalks, and welcoming parks in every neighborhood. Council reviews proposals in public, and residents can follow the agenda and comment before a vote.

lines.speaker: Mayor Rivera
lines.text: Where would you like to listen first? Your choice guides the next canvassing focus.

choices.text: Talk with residents in the neighborhood
choices.npcResponseText: Start by listening at the doors and public spaces where neighbors already gather.
choices.educationalNote: Respect a resident's choice to talk or decline, and record themes without promising outcomes.

choices.text: Hear from people along Main Street
choices.npcResponseText: Business owners and workers can describe how street changes affect daily life.
choices.educationalNote: Ask open questions and include workers, customers, and people who do not own businesses.

choices.text: Visit the public services district
choices.npcResponseText: Libraries, transit stops, and schools are useful places to hear a wider range of needs.
choices.educationalNote: Public engagement should be accessible and welcoming to people with different schedules and needs.
